title: Name the guest's locked model by its slug, as the picker does
body: A guest's locked model button read "Opus 5.5 Fast" while the model picker lists models by slug. It now shows `claude-opus-5.5`, the same label a signed-in user sees for that model (the picker shows the `-fast` id as its base with fast on), and falls back to `claude-opus-5.5-fast` when the catalog has no base entry.

title: Make menu popovers modal so a click in the preview closes them
body:
With the model picker (or another menu) open, clicking the design preview left it open. The preview is an iframe, and clicks inside it never reach the parent document, so Radix never saw an outside click.

The menu popovers (model picker, attach, export, account, chat menu) are now `modal`. While open, Radix disables pointer events outside the content, so a click on the preview lands on the parent document and Radix dismisses the menu on its own, as `DropdownMenu` does by default. The first click on the preview with a menu open only closes the menu. The hover help popover next to the free-prompt count stays non-modal, since the pointer has to travel from the icon to its link.

Checked in the browser with an iframe on the page: with `modal` a click inside it closes the attach menu, without it the menu stays open.

title: Keep the reasoning-effort target one width while cycling levels
body:
In the model picker, clicking the effort level cycles it (default, low, medium, high, max). The target was as wide as its label and right-aligned, so going from `default` to `max` shrank it from the left and quick repeated clicks missed it.

It is now as wide as the longest level for that model (`Nch`, the label is monospace), right-aligned, with a little padding for a bigger hit area. Enter and Space also cycle it now, with a focus ring; it had `role="button"` but no keyboard handling.

title: Stop stalling the page after sign-out by dropping Clear-Site-Data
body:
Sign-out clears the UI optimistically and the server now answers fast, but the page still froze for seconds afterwards. The response carried `Clear-Site-Data: "cache"`, and Chrome honors it by scanning its whole disk cache, not just this origin's entries, before the page can move on. The bigger the browser's cache, the longer the freeze.

The header existed to purge design previews cached for a year (`private, max-age=31536000, immutable`), so the next person on a shared browser could not load them. The live preview is now `private, no-cache` with an `ETag` per chat and revision: the browser keeps a copy but revalidates it through this route's session check first. A signed-in reload costs an empty 304; a signed-out browser gets nothing from its cache. Sign-out drops `Clear-Site-Data`.

Tests cover the 304 revalidation and the absence of the header on sign-out.

title: Drop the billing notice for signed-in users on a paid model
body: A signed-in user on a model other than Opus 5.5 Fast saw "Uses your billing team. ?" above the input whenever free prompts remained. That case is gone. The notice now shows only the free-prompt count (guest or signed-in on Opus 5.5 Fast) and, for a guest who used them up, "Free prompts are used. Sign in".

title: Show a listed chat's model the moment it is opened
body:
Switching chats showed a skeleton in the model picker for a moment, until `/api/model?session=…` answered: a function round trip plus a Redis read on every switch.

The sidebar already reads each chat's state from Redis in one pipeline. The same `hmget` now also returns the stored model, effort and fast flag, and the composer applies them on the first frame of a switch, with no request and no skeleton. A chat the list does not have yet (opened by URL before the sidebar loads) still asks the server as before.

An empty stored model means the app default. On a switch it is applied as is, never replaced with the previous chat's selection; a test covers that no write goes to the chat.

title: Fix the findings from the security review
body:
Fixes the issues from the recent security review of fx0. Each fix is its own commit, so this can be reviewed one commit at a time.

## Fixes

- **Paid turns bill the login and team that sent them** (6266830). A turn pins its sender's funding when it starts, so a paid turn can't be billed to whoever touched the chat last.
- **Signing out only affects that login** (ca038b9). Sign-out deletes only that login's chat credentials, and no longer cancels turns: libfx's cancel stops whichever turn is open, which may be another login's. A turn that login funded stops at its next model request with "Sign in again". Another device's turns keep going.
- **A running turn rebinds before each model request** (9c0441a). With many chats open, a reply can no longer pick up another chat's funding.
- **A signed-out login's cookie stops working everywhere** (4c391d1). Pages and API routes check the sign-out marker on every request, and a signed-out grant is never refreshed. If Redis is down, the check fails closed.
- **A design's CSP always lands first in `<head>`** (8c5b0b0). Design HTML is normalized once (trimmed, canonical doctype), and that one value is validated, stored and rendered. A leading U+00A0 used to push the CSP into `<body>`, which let a design open nested frames. Errors spell out invisible characters so the agent can fix them on retry.
- **Designs ask before opening links** (556d93f). The preview wrapper only forwards the request. fx0 shows the whole address in a dialog and opens it only from a real click. Only https is allowed, with no credentials in the address, up to 2,048 characters.
- **Subagents share the turn's 64 model steps** (75ae9d8). Steps are counted per turn in Redis, and a retry counts once. Before this, one free prompt could reach about 4,000 model calls.
- **The libfx wake route stays private** (1f85c40). On Vercel only Vercel Queues can call it, but the bundled queue client trusts the delivery it is handed. A test now fails if the route loses its queue trigger or another route starts serving the wake handler.
- **Turn bookkeeping commits with the turn's transcript lines** (00f02da). The running marker, the turn's history work and the design it left are written in the same Redis script as its lines. A history write that fails is retried by later followers for 7 days, and each turn's history keeps the design version that turn actually left.
- **Stop always reaches libfx** (97a388f), even when fx0's running marker is missing or has expired. The screen says when there was nothing to stop.
- **A closed event stream ignores late journal failures** (788d138), instead of writing to a closed controller and leaving an unhandled rejection.
- **Back to `/` shows a new chat** (da96024), instead of requesting a `lobby` chat and leaving the previous chat active. Unsent text is kept.

Also included: the activity timer no longer resets when you switch chats and come back (ad74ee1).

The preview-cache finding isn't in this PR because #4 already fixed it.

## Testing

| Command | Result |
|---|---|
| `npm run typecheck` | pass |
| `npm run test:core` | 122/122 |
| `npm run test:auth` | 234/234 |
| `npm run test:trial:integration` | 1/1 |
| `npm run test:credential:integration` (new) | 1/1 |
| `npm run test:budget:integration` (new) | 1/1 |
| `npm run test:turns:integration` (new) | 4/4 |
| `npm run test:artifact:browser` (new, needs local Chrome) | 1/1, 28 cases |
| `tests/journal.integration.mjs` against local Redis through the new `tests/fixtures/redis-rest.mjs` | 14/14 |
| `npm run build` | pass |

The new integration tests need a local `redis-server` and no remote services.

## Deploy and rollback

- No migrations and no new environment variables.
- Paid funding records live under a new `paid-funding:` key (a409e2a). Today's code reads only `funding:`, and refuses a chat's unpinned paid turns once that holds any record, so after a rollback to `1337da0` paid chats bill the way they do now.
- A paid turn already running or queued at deploy time has no funding record. It keeps billing the chat's latest credential, as it does today, even after a follow-up. Every message since the deploy is pinned before libfx sees it, so any newer turn without a record bills nothing.
- Checked by loading `1337da0`'s `lib/turn-credential.ts` next to this branch's against one in-memory Redis: rollback, deploy, trial-chat, sign-out and deletion cases, 12/12.
- The running marker keeps its key, format and 30-minute expiry, so old and new projectors read each other's.
- Tabs opened before the deploy ignore a design's link requests until they reload. If you roll back, history writes still waiting to be retried are dropped (they expire within 7 days).

## Tested on the preview

Signed in on the preview deployment for a409e2a, using new chats only, with the preview's server logs checked afterwards:

- A paid reply and a follow-up each bill the sender's team; a model the team's Gateway allowlist blocks fails with Gateway's 403, as before.
- The rendered design starts with `<!doctype html><meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" ...>`, the only CSP, first in `<head>`; past versions too.
- A design link opens fx0's dialog with the full address and Cancel focused. Cancel or Enter opens nothing, a second ask within 2 seconds is ignored, a click on Open link in its first half second is ignored, and Open link opens one tab with no opener and no referrer.
- The activity counter keeps counting across a switch to another chat and back (33s, 32s after the send).
- Stop says "Stop requested.", logs `turn:cancel`, and the reply ends within a few seconds.
- Back from a chat to `/` shows a new chat, keeps the unsent text, loads no chat, and the next message goes to `/api/prompt?session=new`.
- Each finished reply's design is in history at its own revision (revisions 1 to 4 checked).
- After sign-out, the cookies copied before it are signed out on `/api/auth/me`, `/api/sessions` (401) and `/`, and the grant cookie is cleared.
- Preview logs for the session: no `funding:refused`, `turn:step-limit`, `history:*:error`, `follow:error` or `artifact:unrenderable`; the only errors are two sign-in attempts that granted no team.

## Notes

- This conflicts with #5 only in `tests/guest-ui.test.mjs`. A test added here sits next to one that #5 renames.
- libfx should verify queue deliveries before running them. That belongs in libfx and isn't part of this PR.
- Existing history rows that might hold a wrong design version haven't been audited.

title: Show thinking once the server accepts a prompt
body:

title: The 64-step limit per turn never stops anything
body:
## Summary

The README says a turn stops after 64 model steps, so an agent stuck in a loop can't run up a bill. That limit doesn't work in production. A turn can make as many model requests as it wants.

## What goes wrong

To count steps, fx0 reads the request it is about to send to the model. It only understands the request when it arrives as plain text. The libfx library sends it in a different format (raw bytes). fx0 doesn't recognize it, so it can't see how far along the turn is. Every step of the turn gets counted as the first step, and the count never reaches 64.

## How I checked

- I ran the real libfx package and looked at what it sends to fx0. It sends raw bytes every time.
- I sent 100 steps of one turn through fx0's real request handling. When the request was plain text, as in the tests, the limit stopped it at 64. When the request was raw bytes, as libfx really sends it, all 100 went through.
- The same happened against a real Redis, where the counter stayed at 1 for all 100 steps.

## Why the tests didn't catch it

All the tests send the request as plain text, so they pass. None of them send it the way libfx does.

## Impact

- A turn that gets stuck in a loop, or is pushed into one by a malicious web page the agent reads, keeps running until the user presses Stop.
- For signed-in users, the extra requests are billed to their own team.
- For free-trial users, they are billed to the deployment's own gateway key. The five-free-prompts-per-IP rule limits how many turns can start, but not how long each one runs.
- Subagents have the same problem, so they don't count toward the limit either.

## Suggested direction

- Make the step counter understand the format libfx actually sends.
- If a request can't be understood, don't let it skip the limit.
- Change the tests to use the same format as libfx.

title: Count model steps when libfx sends the request body as bytes
body:
Fixes #9

## Problem

A turn is meant to stop after 64 model steps. That limit never triggered in production.

To count steps, fx0 reads the request it is about to send to the model, but it only understood requests that arrived as plain text. libfx sends them as bytes (a `Buffer`). fx0 could not read the conversation, so every step of a turn was counted as the first step and the count never reached 64.

The tests passed because they all sent the request as plain text.

## Fix

- Read the request whether it arrives as text or as bytes.
- If a request still cannot be read, count it as a step of its own instead of sharing one name with every other unreadable request, so it can never skip the limit.
- Tests now send the request as bytes, like libfx does, and cover each form a body can take plus the unreadable case.

## Checked

- With the old code, the new tests fail, including the existing 64-step test once it sends bytes.
- With the fix, all tests in `tests/libfx-agent.test.mjs` pass, along with `test:auth`, the turn budget integration test and the type check.
- A request body captured from the real libfx package is read correctly, and a resend of the same step still counts once.

title: Stop the phone zooming into the prompt and label the pane switch
body:
On a phone, tapping the prompt made iOS Safari zoom in and the page stayed panned sideways afterwards, even after the keyboard closed. Safari does this for any focused field under 16px; the prompt and the model search rendered at 14px.

- Text fields render at 16px on coarse pointers only (`@media (pointer: coarse)`), so desktop keeps 14px. Chosen over `maximum-scale=1`, which would also block pinch zoom for people who rely on it.
- The phone header's pane toggle was an icon that read as a sidebar control. It is now a text button that names the pane the tap goes to: `preview` while in the chat, `chat` while in the preview.
- The header drops to 8px side padding and a tighter gap below `md`, so the chat title keeps its room next to the wider label. Desktop spacing is unchanged.
- Removes the now-unused Tooltip import.

Verified with Playwright emulating iPhone 14 Pro and iPad Pro 11: the prompt measures 16px and `scrollWidth` equals the viewport width in both pane states; desktop still measures 14px.

title: Count model steps when libfx sends the request body as bytes
body:
## Summary

- The 64-step limit now counts a turn's steps when libfx sends the model request body as bytes, which it always does. A turn stuck in a loop stops after 64 model requests instead of running until Stop.
- A model request whose body cannot be read counts as a new step each time, so it can never skip the limit.

Fixes #9. This is @akramcodez's fix from #10, landed from a branch in this repo so it can deploy; they are credited as co-author.

title: Send long prompts whole instead of cutting them at 4,000 characters
body:
## Summary

- `/api/prompt` cut every prompt's text at 4,000 characters (`text.slice(0, 4000)`) without telling anyone, so a long paste reached the model only partly. Text now goes through whole, up to 256 KB.
- Text over 256 KB is refused as a whole with a 413 and a clear message, never cut.
- The composer checks the same limit before sending and shows the error under the prompt, so the draft stays put.
- The guest draft that survives sign-in uses the same limit (it was 64 KB).
- The limit lives in one place, `lib/prompt-limits.ts`. With 3 MiB of images, their previews and a DESIGN.md, a full prompt still fits in one function request body (4.5 MB) and well inside libfx's 8 MiB durable input.

## Verification

- `npm run test:auth`: 237 pass, 0 fail. Includes a new route test: 256 KB of text reaches the agent whole, and text past the limit gets a 413 before any reservation or agent work.
- `npm run test:core`: 122 pass, 0 fail.
- `npm run typecheck`: passes.

title: Let published designs show their embedded images, fonts and media
body:
## Summary

- A published design is a `data:` document framed by `/api/artifact-frame`. That frame inherits the wrapper response's CSP on top of the design's embedded CSP, and a resource loads only if both allow it.
- The wrapper CSP had `default-src 'none'` with no `img-src`, `font-src` or `media-src`. Every published design lost its `data:` images, fonts and media, even though the validator accepts them and the draft preview shows them.
- The wrapper policy is now `DESIGN_FRAME_CSP` in `lib/design-artifact.ts` and allows the same `data:` sources as the embedded policy. Remote sources, `connect-src`, frames and scripts are unchanged.

## Verification

- New Chrome test (`npm run test:artifact:browser`) renders a published design under both policies with the production frame attributes: an embedded `data:` image loads and a remote image is refused by CSP. It fails against the previous wrapper policy.
- `npm run typecheck` passes.
- `npm run test:core`: 122 pass, 0 fail.
- `npm run test:auth`: 237 pass, 0 fail.
- `npm run test:artifact:browser`: 2 pass, 0 fail.

title: Let designs show remote images by embedding them before they run
body: ## Summary - A published design could only use `data:` images. Any `https:` image the model wrote was rejected at publish. - Remote `https:` images are now accepted where they are images: ``, ``, ``, `

title: Keep a design's remote images in the browser cache across revisions
body:
## Summary

- Every preview revision carried its remote images inside the HTML, so a one-line edit downloaded every photo again.
- `/api/artifact-frame` now replaces each remote image with a marker (`fx0-image-<nonce>-<n>`), using a nonce that is new on every response, so text in the design cannot name one. It passes the wrapper the list of images, each with a URL on `/api/artifact-image` that is signed for this chat.
- The wrapper loads those images, swaps each marker for its `data:` image within the 4 MiB budget (counted for every place an image is written), and only then frames the design. A missing image becomes a blank image.
- `/api/artifact-image` serves only the chat's owner, and only URLs `artifact-frame` signed for that chat (HMAC-SHA256 over the chat and the URL, with a key derived from `SESSION_SECRET`). It cannot be used to fetch arbitrary addresses. The image comes from the shared cache that the draft prefetch warms, with `private, max-age=86400`. The URL is the same for every revision, so the browser reuses the image. A refusal or a failed image returns 404 with `no-store`.
- The design still has no network. Its own CSP keeps `connect-src 'none'` and its frame is `credentialless`. Only the wrapper may connect, and only to the image route (`connect-src <origin>/api/artifact-image`, added only when the design has images).
- The `artifact-frame` response no longer carries images, so it is small again and no longer needs streaming.

## Verification

- `npm run typecheck` and `next build` pass.
- `npm run test:core`: 138 pass, 0 fail. Covers markers in document order up to the count budget, the per-response nonce, a typed or forged marker staying inert, and signatures refused for another chat, another URL or a tampered value.
- `npm run test:auth`: 238 pass, 0 fail. The image route returns 404 without caching for another user's chat (even with a URL signed for it), a missing URL, a missing or forged signature, and a signature made for another chat. It returns 401 without a session.
- `npm run test:artifact:browser`: 3 pass, 0 fail. The real wrapper is served with its CSP header:
  - marked images are embedded and decode;
  - a later revision of the same design embeds its image from the browser cache, with one request to the route in total;
  - a design past 2 MiB renders;
  - one 1 MiB image repeated six times embeds four copies;
  - the design cannot connect to the route or load a remote image.

  The cache and budget checks fail when the wrapper's fetch bypasses the cache or the budget is removed.

title: Resize attached images in the browser and check them on the server
body:
## Summary

- A Retina screenshot or a phone photo was usually over the 3 MiB image limit, so the composer refused it. HEIC and SVG files passed the composer and failed in libfx after the message was sent. The server accepted any string as an image.
- **Composer** (`components/attach-image.ts`): each attached image is decoded, scaled to at most 2048 px on its long side and encoded as WebP. It steps down in quality, then size (1600 and 1200 px), until it is under 700 KB.
  - Where the browser cannot encode WebP, a transparent image becomes PNG and an opaque one JPEG.
  - A small PNG, JPEG, WebP or GIF is sent as is, so nothing is re-encoded and a GIF keeps its animation.
  - HEIC is converted where the browser can decode it; elsewhere it gets a clear error.
  - Files over 40 MB or 60 megapixels are refused before drawing.
  - The thumbnail is made at attach time instead of on send.
- **Server** (`lib/prompt-images.ts`): before any reservation or write, `/api/prompt` accepts only canonical base64 PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP. The bytes must match the declared type, and the header must give sane dimensions (at most 8000 px on a side; baseline and progressive JPEG and all three WebP layouts are read without decoding). The 8-image and 3 MiB limits are now shared with the composer in `lib/prompt-limits.ts`.
- Thumbnails are stored only when every image has one, so a missing thumbnail can no longer shift the rest onto the wrong images.

## Verification

- `npm run typecheck` and `next build` pass.
- `npm run test:core`: 142 pass, 0 fail. New `tests/prompt-images.test.mjs` covers:
  - dimensions from every supported header;
  - wrong or unsupported types, SVG labeled as PNG, missing padding, whitespace and non-canonical padding bits;
  - truncated headers, more than 8000 px, more than 8 images and more than 3 MiB;
  - all-or-nothing thumbnails.
- `npm run test:auth`: 238 pass, 0 fail.
- `npm run test:artifact:browser`: 4 pass, 0 fail. New `tests/attach-image.browser.mjs` runs the composer's code in Chrome:
  - a 4000×3000 image becomes 2048×1536 WebP under 700 KB, with a JPEG thumbnail;
  - without WebP, a transparent image becomes PNG and an opaque one JPEG under 700 KB;
  - a small JPEG and a GIF are sent unchanged;
  - a non-image is refused.

  The test fails if the 2048 px limit is removed.

title: Let a design show the images the user attached
Upload attached images while libfx admits the prompt, and keep them five minutes
body:
## Summary

- **Upload in parallel with admission.** An image prompt stored its files in Blob before handing the prompt to libfx, so every image prompt waited for the upload before admission started.
  - `/api/prompt` now reserves the caps and creates the handles first. A cap still refuses the prompt before anything is stored.
  - The upload then runs while the prompt is journaled and admitted by libfx; the model's message carries the references from the start.
  - Once libfx has accepted the prompt, `submitPrompt` waits for the upload (a new `assets` stage in `prompt:stages`). Admission takes longer than the upload, so this wait is normally zero.
  - If the files could not be stored, the admitted turn is cancelled and the chat shows "The attached images could not be stored. Send the message again." Files and quota are cleaned up as before, so the model never works with references that do not exist.
- **Browser cache for attached images.** They are now kept for five minutes (`private, max-age=300`, with the ETag), so a design's edits no longer wait on a revalidation round trip per image before the wrapper can frame the design. After five minutes a 304 still checks ownership and the chat's manifest without a Blob download. Deleting the chat stops an image at the next revalidation; until then only the browser that already had it could open its exact URL.
- **Draft prefetch off the stream path.** The image prefetch now scans each draft on the next turn of the event loop instead of inside the stream's delta callback, so a very large design cannot delay tokens on their way to libfx.

## Verification

- `npm run typecheck` and `next build` pass.
- `npm run test:core`: 160 pass, 0 fail. New runtime tests cover:
  - libfx receives the prompt, with its `fx0-asset:` references, before the upload has finished;
  - an upload that fails after admission cancels the turn and shows the error. This test fails without the cancellation.
- `npm run test:auth`: 241 pass, 0 fail. The attachment route test covers the five-minute cache, 304s without Blob downloads, and refusal after deletion, for another user and without a session.
- `npm run test:artifact:browser`: 4 pass, 0 fail.

title: Chat replies can send private content to an attacker through Markdown images
body: ## Summary The agent's chat replies are shown as Markdown, and Markdown can load images from any website. There is no Content Security Policy on the app, so nothing stops those images from loading. A web page the agent reads can tell it to write an image link that carries the user's private chat content to an attacker's server, with no click needed. ## What goes wrong - The agent has `web_fetch` and web search, so it reads pages that anyone can write. - Its replies are drawn with `` (`components/markdown.tsx`, used from `components/thread.tsx`). By default it turns `![x](https://...)` into a real ``. - fx0 sends no `Content-Security-Policy` on the app itself. `next.config.mjs` sets no headers, and there is no `proxy.ts` or `middleware.ts`. - A malicious page can tell the model to end its reply with an image link whose address contains the user's earlier messages. If the model follows it, the browser requests that address as soon as the reply streams in, and the attacker's server gets the data in the URL. The design preview is well protected: sandboxed frame, CSP, `connect-src 'none'`. The chat transcript has none of that. ## How I checked - I read the render path and searched the repo for any CSP, header config, proxy or middleware. There is none for the app origin. - I have not run this end to end against a live deployment. The behaviour comes from `react-markdown`'s default of rendering remote images, so it's worth confirming in a browser. ## Why the tests didn't catch it The CSP tests only cover the design frame and the image and export routes. Nothing checks what the chat text can load. ## Impact - Anything in the model's context can leave the browser: the user's prompts, an uploaded `DESIGN.md`, earlier fetched pages, the design HTML. - It needs only that the agent reads one hostile page, such as a search result or a link the user pasted. - No credentials are in the context, so this is a privacy leak, not an account takeover.

title: The five-free-prompts-per-IP limit resets for every IPv6 address
body:
## Summary

The README says the five free prompts are "five per IP across chats and browsers, with no periodic refill". On IPv6 that isn't true. The limit counts each exact address, and one user usually controls billions of addresses, so they can get five free prompts again and again on the deployment's own gateway key.

## What goes wrong

- `trialIpHash` in `lib/trial.ts` hashes the full client address from `x-forwarded-for`. For IPv6 that is the whole /128.
- A home or office connection normally gets at least a /64, which is about 18 quintillion addresses. Using a different source address gives a fresh bucket with a fresh allowance of five.
- Each admitted prompt is paid for with the server's `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` on Opus 5.5 Fast, and a turn can run up to 64 model steps plus web search and subagents.
- BotID is the only other check. It looks at whether the client is a bot, not at how many addresses it has used.

## How I checked

- I read `trialIpHash` and how `app/api/prompt/route.ts` uses it. `canonical` is the whole address, so two addresses in the same /64 get different buckets.
- I have not run this against a deployment. I haven't tested how BotID treats a real browser that changes address between prompts.

## Why the tests didn't catch it

The trial tests don't send two addresses from the same prefix and expect them to share a bucket.

## Impact

- The free-trial allowance can be reset by anyone with an IPv6 prefix, so spend on the deployment's key isn't capped.
- This is a billing risk for whoever runs the deployment, and it breaks the guarantee in the README.

title: Stop chat replies from loading remote images
body: Fixes #21 ## Problem Chat replies are drawn as Markdown, and Markdown turns `![x](https://...)` into a real ``. The app sends no Content Security Policy, so the browser loads it. A page the agent reads can tell the model to write an image link that contains the user's earlier messages, and the browser sends that address to the attacker's server as soon as the reply streams in. ## Fix - Chat replies no longer render images at all. - Every page now sends `Content-Security-Policy: img-src 'self' data: blob:`, so the browser refuses third-party images even if one reaches the page some other way. The app only shows its own `data:` and `blob:` previews. - Raw HTML in a reply was already shown as text, and a test now covers that too. ## Checked - Before the fix, rendering a reply with a remote image produced an `` pointing at the other host, plus a preload hint for it. After the fix, neither is produced. - The two new tests (reply text in `tests/html-ui.test.mjs`, the header in `tests/core.test.mjs`) fail on the old code and pass with the fix. - `test:core` has 158 passing and 0 failing. title: Share one free-prompt allowance across an IPv6 /64
body:
Fixes #22

## Problem

The five free prompts are meant to be five per IP, with no refill. For IPv6, fx0 counted each exact address. One home or office connection controls a whole /64, so using a different address gave a fresh allowance of five, paid for by the deployment's gateway key.

## Fix

- For IPv6, the free-prompt bucket is now the /64 prefix, so every address in one /64 shares one allowance.
- An IPv4-mapped IPv6 address (`::ffff:a.b.c.d`) uses its IPv4 address, so those clients do not all collapse into one bucket.
- IPv4 behaves as before.
- The README limit now says an IPv6 /64 counts as one IP.

The global daily cap on sponsored spend from the issue is not part of this change.

## Checked

- The two new tests (`tests/trial.test.mjs`) fail on the old code and pass with the fix. They cover addresses in the same /64 sharing a bucket, neighbouring prefixes and IPv4 addresses staying apart, mapped addresses, and `trialIpHash` itself.
- `test:auth` has 243 passing and 0 failing, `test:trial:integration` passes, and the type check passes.
- `test:core` has 157 passing and 0 failing. The 3 cancelled tests are DNS lookups that cannot run in my sandbox, and they are cancelled the same way on `main`.
- I have not tried this against a deployment or with BotID.

title: Click an element in the preview to edit it or tell the agent about it
body:
## Summary

Let people click an element in the preview and change it directly, or tell the agent about that exact element. Today every change, even one colour or one line of copy, goes through a full model turn.

## Problem

- The only way to change a design is to describe the change in the chat, and the model has to find the right place in the HTML on its own.
- A small tweak costs a whole turn, which is slow and spends tokens, and for signed-in users it is billed to their team.
- Describing "the second button in the pricing card" in words is awkward and easy for the model to get wrong.
- Other design tools, such as v0 (Design Mode) and Lovable (visual edits), let you select an element in the preview and edit it.

## Proposal

- Add a select mode to the preview. Hovering outlines an element, and clicking selects it.
- With an element selected, the person can do either of these:
  - Type a request in the composer. The message carries the selected element, so the agent knows exactly what "this" is and can use `edit_design` on it.
  - Change simple things in place, such as text, colour, font size and spacing, with no model call. The change applies at once and becomes a new version.

## How it could work

- `parseOpeningTags` in `lib/design-artifact.ts` already knows where every tag sits in the stored source. The copy of the design prepared for preview can add a `data-fx0-id` to each tag. The stored design is not touched.
- The preview frame already runs fx0's own bootstrap script and talks to the app by `postMessage` with a per-load token. The same channel can carry "element hovered" and "element selected" messages.
- A new route takes an element id and an edit, maps the id back to the source range of that tag in the current revision, applies the change, and saves it through the existing `publishDesignArtifact`. Versions, history and the draft fence then work as they do now.
- A person's edit is recorded as its own version, with no turn, so it can be reopened like any other.
- The selected element is sent to the model as part of the message text, using the same exact-match rules `edit_design` already has.

## Scope

- Select mode in the preview, plus a small panel for text, colour, font size and spacing.
- The route that applies a direct edit, with a check that the revision the person saw is still the current one.
- Sending the selected element along with a chat message.
- Tests for id assignment, mapping an id back to the source, edits that collide with a turn publishing at the same time, and messages from the frame.

## Not included

- Dragging, resizing or reordering elements.
- Editing designs that use scripts to build their own markup, beyond what is in the stored HTML.
- Mobile preview editing.

## Risks and open questions

- The design runs its own scripts inside the sandboxed frame, so it can send fake select messages. That should only be able to affect that design, and the app should treat every message from the frame as untrusted.
- If the agent is publishing while the person edits, one of them has to win cleanly. A revision check on the edit route would reject the older one with a clear message.
- Text that scripts rewrite at run time can look editable but not match the source. Those elements should be shown as not editable.
- It is a large change, so it may be better to land select-and-tell-the-agent first and direct property edits second.

Add three deterministic regression tests that execute the served wrapper with a controlled clock: delayed heartbeats after a tab return, timer suspension before the visibility event, and recovery from continued foreground silence. The two tab-return cases failed before the fix.

title: Preserve preview state across compatible design updates
body:
## Summary

Update compatible published designs in place instead of restarting the preview's scripts for every revision.

- Patch existing stylesheets, inline styles on uniquely identified elements, and identified leaf text after checking the authored source, embedded render, and live values. Keep unedited interactive state and existing nodes in place.
- Retain the double-buffered reload path for script, structural, unsupported, or conflicting changes. Keep the published design visible while the next revision is prepared.
- Correlate updates with their revisions and document identities, cancel superseded preparation, bound stalled payload/image work, and recover from the last confirmed snapshot.
- Preserve the existing ownership checks, opaque script sandbox, CSP, and image preparation. Hide published frames, retained drafts, and link dialogs when access is revoked.

### Follow-up corrections

- Keep the existing stylesheet and shared unchanged CSS rules across disjoint edits, insertions, and deletions. Apply separate preflighted splices from right to left. Ambiguous or reordered shared rules and replacements of populated grouping rules use the reload path instead of invalidating cached references.
- Count visible, unsuspended execution for the full-load paint deadline and query the wrapper's status on resume. A replacement that loaded in a hidden tab stays mounted until it can paint. Visible stalled loads still expire; payload acquisition and image preparation keep their separate wall-clock deadlines.

## Verification

All checks ran on this preview-only branch with Node 24.22.0 and exited with code 0.

- `node --experimental-strip-types --test tests/core.test.mjs tests/route-security.test.mjs tests/html-ui.test.mjs tests/auth-ui.test.mjs tests/design-draft.test.mjs`: 152 tests passed.
- `node --experimental-strip-types --test tests/preview-update.browser.mjs`: 21 tests passed, none skipped. Covers compatible edits, cached sheet/rule/declaration references, disjoint edits and insertions/deletions, conservative fallback for ambiguous or grouped changes, CSSOM conflicts, cancellation, deadlines, revision ordering, recovery, hydration, authorization revocation, and embedded images beyond 2 MiB. A real tab switch stays hidden for 21 seconds, preserves the loaded replacement, and reveals it without restarting on return; a genuinely stalled visible load still expires.
- The middle-rule identity and hidden-tab timeout regressions failed before the corrections.
- `node node_modules/next/dist/bin/next build`: passed, including TypeScript.
- `node tests/local-auth-smoke.mjs`: passed against the production build with simulated external services.
- Temporary Chrome verification against the actual Next-built artifact routes and serialized updater: 19 checks passed. Disjoint CSS edits preserved the cached intermediate rule; a real click still changed the displayed input opacity through its original declaration. The compatible update also preserved the same document and nodes, one script boot, slide 4, scroll at 900 px, input, focus, and selection. Only identity and stored data were simulated. Next stderr stayed empty.
- `git diff --check`: passed.

## Scope

title: Let fx0 inspect its generated designs with screenshots
body:
## Purpose

Temporary preview experiment: let a user ask fx0 to build a design, inspect what it actually rendered, and correct it using screenshots. Keep this PR in draft while we validate the feedback loop on a Vercel preview; do not merge it just to try it.

## What is included

- Capture the on-screen preview at its current revision, with a hidden-preview fallback when needed. Return viewport screenshots or full-page tiles as **image tool-result content sent to the model**, not just HTML or screenshot metadata.
- Validate and authorize capture uploads, coordinate the request through Redis/events, and show capture activity/timing in the transcript.
- Vendor the corrected fast-html-to-image browser fork from fast-snap `2e119bc` (MIT). The checked-in bundle is self-contained: preview builds do not need access to the private fast-snap repository or a new npm package.
- Preserve main's background-tab/suspended-timer recovery behavior while holding the watchdog during capture; add a regression test for the combined behavior.

## Local verification

Node 24.22.1, Next.js 16.4.2:

- `npm ci --no-audit --no-fund` — passed.
- `npm run test:core` — 170 passed.
- `npm run test:auth` — 246 passed, including capture ownership and upload validation.
- `npm run test:artifact:browser` — 5 passed in real Chrome, including a hidden preview photographing its viewport and full page under the production CSP without network access.

- `npm run test:smoke` — passed against the production build with fake services; no remote credentials/services used.

No real model request, real sign-in, or paid billing flow was exercised locally. Those remain part of the manual preview check.

## Try on the preview

1. Open the Vercel preview, sign in if needed, and start a **new chat** with an image-capable model (the default Opus is suitable).
2. Keep that fx0 tab open and visible. Ask:

> Build a landing page for a coffee shop with a hero, menu, and contact section. Then use screenshot_design to inspect the result. Check alignment, contrast, spacing, and clipping; fix any visible issues and take another screenshot to verify the changes. Do not claim you inspected the result if you could not obtain an image.

title: Avoid the JSON preflight on the first design preview
body:
## Context

Stacked on #30, not `main`. This PR removes the redundant JSON request on the first design preview load and includes regression coverage plus a reproducible real-network A/B harness. #30 remains unchanged.

## Changes

- Load HTML directly when no confirmed preview document exists. Keep JSON acquisition for hot updates of an existing document.
- Report failed iframe loads through the preview message channel, preserving 401/403 authentication gating and retryable 404/422/503 feedback, including failures before hydration.
- Reject stale live revisions before running old design code. Preserve ownership checks, private cache policy, renewed cookies, and the client-side closed-auth gate.
- Share the existing production-component browser fixture between regression tests and the live A/B runner.
- Run live measurement code in the page's JavaScript context: requests issued directly from AppleEvents did not appear in the page's Resource Timing entries. Preserve partial clocks, available requests, and capture diagnostics on failure.
- Pin the owned test window and reject changes in source, viewport, request order, or image dimensions. No benchmark switch or artificial latency enters production.

## Real-network A/B results

Completed October 26, 2026, in authenticated normal Chrome against the deployed Vercel backend, with no injected network delay.

| Metric — median | JSON → HTML | Direct HTML | Improvement |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Requests before capture | 2 | 1 | 50% |
| Preview ready | 663.4 ms | 453.5 ms | 31.6% |
| Image ready | 710.8 ms | 503.5 ms | 29.2% |

- 30 measured pairs: 15 AB and 15 BA, shuffled with recorded seed `20261026`.
- Four warmup captures excluded; 64 successful captures in the completed run. No failed measured samples were discarded or retried within that run.
- The direct-HTML flow was faster in all 30 pairs. Median paired reduction: 214.5 ms; exploratory 95% percentile-bootstrap interval: 167.7–251.4 ms.
- The removed JSON request had a median duration of 212.45 ms.
- The source revision and HTML SHA-256 matched before and after every trial. All captured images were 1000×720 WebP files of 28,312 bytes.
- Authenticated runtime logs also confirmed successful screenshot tool results for revisions 1 and 2 in a real model-driven conversation; the controlled benchmark does not assess visual correctness.

### Scope and limitations

A reconstructs the old JSON-first flow by removing the direct-load guard from a temporary compile of the current component. B runs the current component unchanged. Both use the same actual backend, authentication, stored design, frame renderer, and capture engine. This isolates the client flow; it is not a comparison of two independently deployed application bundles.

The measured interval starts when the fixture updates the preview's source revision and ends when the encoded image Blob is available. Image decoding is validated afterward. Server publication, model generation, upload, and delivery to the model are excluded.

This is one image-free design and one network path with warm resources/connections, not a general performance guarantee. The reused page may retain timers from its original app. Raw private HTML, chat identifiers, cookies, tokens, and image bytes are not published as benchmark data.

## Verification

All commands completed successfully (exit 0), using Node 24.22.1:

- `node --experimental-strip-types --test tests/preview-live-ab.test.mjs`: 13 tests; rerun before committing.
- `node --experimental-strip-types --test tests/preview-update.browser.mjs`: 33 Chrome tests after the fixture extraction and runner fixes.
- Live A/B runner with `--pairs 30 --seed 20261026`: 30 complete measured pairs plus warmups, independently checked for source identity, request counts/statuses, image dimensions, and paired medians.
- Syntax checks for the new runner and shared fixture; `git diff --check`.

The production optimization also passed 261 auth tests, 170 core tests, typecheck, build, and a mocked production smoke before the harness-only commit. Those production files are unchanged by the harness commit.

## Reproduce the live measurement

Use an owned, dedicated **normal Chrome test window/tab**, authenticated to this preview and authorized to read the selected chat. Enable **View → Developer → Allow JavaScript from Apple Events**. The runner replaces that test tab's page contents and pins its window bounds; do not use a personal working tab.

Use a stable, image-free design and do not edit it during the run:

```sh
node --experimental-strip-types tests/preview-live-ab.mjs \
  --tab YOUR_TEST_TAB_ID \
  --window YOUR_TEST_WINDOW_ID \
  --session YOUR_OWNED_CHAT_UUID \
  --pairs 30 \
  --seed 20261026 \
  --out /tmp/fx0-preview-live-ab.json
```

The output path must not already exist. The runner performs authenticated reads and local captures only: no model calls, server publication, uploads, credential copying, or access-control bypass. A failure produces a partial report and exits nonzero. Synthetic local comparisons remain opt-in and are separate from the real-network results above.

No merge is required to test the preview.

title: Prevent blank flashes when publishing the first preview
body:
## Summary

- Wait for both the wrapper's `load` event and the isolated design's paint signal before announcing that a published preview is ready.
- Keep the streamed draft visible when the child paints before its wrapper finishes loading, instead of briefly exposing the app background.
- Add a real-browser regression in light and dark modes using the HTML from the reported house generation.

## Reproduction and cause

A recording in the regular Chrome profile captured a roughly 67 ms black flash during the first draft-to-published handoff. The child paint message reached the app before the wrapper's load event; the normal executions delivered those events in the opposite order.

The previous wrapper forwarded the early child paint immediately, allowing React to retire the draft while the wrapper was still loading. The fix gates that existing signal on wrapper load and replays an already-received child paint when load completes. It adds no arbitrary delay and does not change the generated design or its sandbox permissions.

The browser regression holds the wrapper HTTP response open after its scripts run. Its real sandboxed child paints while the wrapper is still loading. Before the fix, the regression fails in both themes because the draft has already been removed. With the fix, the draft remains visible until the response completes, then the interactive preview takes over.

## Verification

```sh
node --experimental-strip-types --test tests/design-artifact.browser.mjs tests/preview-update.browser.mjs tests/core.test.mjs tests/design-draft.test.mjs
```

Result: **107 passed, 0 failed (exit 0)**. `git diff --check` also passed.

## Preview test

1. Open this PR's Vercel preview deployment.
2. Start a fresh chat and send `create a simple house`.
3. Repeat in dark and light modes. Watch the transition from the streamed draft to the published preview: the house should remain visible, without a black/white flash.
4. Check that the published design remains interactive.

The deployed production site has not been changed by this PR.

title: Initialize the lazy SDK backend during chat warm-up
body:
## Purpose

Experimental preview for measuring the cold-start portion of fx0's **Sending** state. This PR targets `main` directly and is independent of the screenshot/first-preview stack (#30 and #31).

**No real latency reduction has been established for this change.** Passing functional tests is not a performance result.

## Change

`warmChat` previously hydrated the chat and constructed the SDK agent. `createFxAgent` is lazy: constructing it does not initialize its durability backend.

The warm-up now awaits `agent().newSessionId()`. In the installed SDK, this initializes the backend and generates an unbound ID; it does not bind a chat, store a session/message, enqueue work, or start a model turn. The ID is discarded. Actual prompt submission still performs its normal funding, persistence, idempotency, and queue-acknowledgement steps.

The warm route also emits:

- `warm:ready` after successful initialization;
- `warm:skipped` on failure, preserving the existing best-effort 204 response;
- a numeric `durationMs` covering the warm handler's hydration/initialization, not request authentication or network time.

The standard logger already supplies the session and server-instance identifiers. No prompts, credentials, or raw failure contents are added to these events.

## Hypothesis and limitations

If warm-up finishes before the send **and the send reaches the same server instance**, SDK initialization can move out of the send's critical path. If the backend is already initialized, the gain may be zero. A different server instance cannot benefit from another instance's in-memory warm-up.

This does not eliminate the SDK's durable admission work or relabel an unaccepted message as Thinking. Existing server traces put the overall SDK admission stage at 497–1,017 ms in five first-prompt samples, but those values are **not** an estimate of this PR's savings.

The existing client warm-up is best effort and requires an authenticated user with a reserved or existing chat. An unreserved guest's first send does not exercise that path. Do not pool those cases into a claimed improvement.

## Verification

Using Node 24.22.1, all completed successfully (exit 0):

- `npm run test:core`: 167 tests, including two new warm-up regressions.
- `npm run test:auth`: 248 tests, including ready/skipped logging and best-effort route behavior.
- `npm run typecheck`.
- `git diff --check`.

The new runtime tests failed against the previous implementation, then passed with the change. They verify that warm-up awaits initialization and does not bind the generated ID, submit events, send prompts, or save execution credentials.

A separate deterministic probe of the installed SDK confirmed that ID generation starts the lazy backend once without storage/queue/model calls, and that prompt acceptance still waits for storage and queue acknowledgement. That probe checks ordering, not latency; its test World is not a measurement of Vercel.

No browser windows or real model calls are required by these regression checks.

## Preview measurement plan

1. Compare a baseline build of `main` with this preview using the same account, model/settings, short text-only prompt, and browser/network conditions.
2. Use an authenticated account. On a new chat, type the prompt and let the existing reservation/warm-up complete before sending. Existing chats can warm while typing too.
3. Correlate `warm:ready` with `prompt:stages` and `prompt:route` by session, timestamps, and **server instance**. A warm response handled by a different instance is not evidence that the sending instance was prepared.
4. Separate cold/first-instance sends, same-instance warmed sends, and already-hot sends. Do not compare their averages as one cohort.
5. Measure browser Send-to-acceptance separately from server `bindMs`, `acceptedMs`, and route stages. Server stages alone do not measure the entire visible Sending interval; active-turn events can also advance the UI.
6. Record sample counts, failures, and unmatched-instance cases before reporting milliseconds or percentages. If nothing improves, report that result.

A real send may incur model charges. Do not automate retries or bypass authentication. This PR does not require foreground control of the user's normal Chrome; further automation should use a properly authenticated headless test profile.

No merge is required to measure the preview. Keep this as a draft until the hypothesis is checked.

title: Warm the prompt's own function while the user types
body:
## Problem

The typing warm-up (`POST /api/warm`) never warmed the instances that serve the prompt. Vercel bundles routes into functions by configuration. `/api/warm` declared `maxDuration = 60` and `/api/prompt` `800`, so they were separate functions.

A cold first prompt pays about 1.5 s of one-time initialization on the instance: Next loads the route, the first Redis and Neon connections open, and libfx's durable backend initializes (~340 ms of module loading). Vercel also routes prompts to started-but-uninitialized processes even while a warm one exists, so this happens in normal use, not only after deploys.

## Change

- `/api/warm` uses `maxDuration = 800`, the same as `/api/prompt`, so both routes share one function.
- `warmChat` also awaits `agent().newSessionId()`, which loads libfx's durable backend and returns an id without writing anything (the id is discarded).
- `tests/function-grouping.test.mjs` fails if the two routes' `maxDuration` ever differ.

Auth is unchanged (`withSessionRoute`, same ownership check). The warm-up writes nothing and never reaches the model. `maxDuration` only caps run time; the route still returns in milliseconds.

## Evidence

Measured on Vercel previews with opt-in tracing (the instrumentation is not part of this PR). Real prompts ran in headless Chrome, with a 3 s pause between the first keystroke and Enter.

**Cold A/B.** Before each pair, both previews were redeployed, so both sides' prompts landed on fresh instances. 6 pairs, 0 failures:

| Metric | Before | After | Paired delta (median) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Sending (send to accepted) | 2580 ms | 1559 ms | **−983 ms (−38 %)**, 6 of 6 pairs faster |
| First text | 3856 ms | 2931 ms | −1056 ms, 5 of 6 pairs faster |
| libfx backend init in the request | 346 ms | 0 ms | |

All 6 "before" prompts were their process's first request. All 6 "after" prompts landed on an instance the warm-up had already served. Every Sending delta exceeds the measured preview noise (~±250 ms).

**Warm A/B.** No redeploys, 4 pairs: no regression (Sending −309 ms, first text −268 ms paired; descriptive only). Even with a warm-up run first, 2 of 4 "before" prompts still paid backend initialization because Vercel spread them across instances; 0 of 4 "after" prompts did.

## Limits

- The full gain needs the warm-up to finish before the send, about 3 s between the first keystroke and Enter. With an instant paste-and-send, the warm-up and the prompt leave together and the gain is partial.
- The per-chat warm-up is still throttled to once a minute per chat, so a quick follow-up does not warm again.
- First-text times on previews are dominated by AI Gateway variance (34 ms to 3.3 s to headers), so Sending is the metric this change moves.

## Verification

- `npm run test:core`: 171 passed, including the new grouping test. It fails when the values differ (checked by mutation).
- `npm run test:auth`: 261 passed.
- `npm run typecheck` and `npm run build`: pass.

title: Open a history chat at once and start its preview with it
body:
## Problem

From a user report: clicking a chat in the history left the URL and the screen on the previous view while the item said "loading". The chat appeared about 1 s later, and the preview took longer still. Expected behavior: move to the new URL at once and render an empty fallback synchronously.

`switchSession` awaited `GET /api/session` before `showSession` and `history.pushState`, and `switchingTo` blocked other clicks meanwhile. The preview (`/api/artifact-frame`) could only start after the snapshot arrived, because it needed the design revision.

## Change

**Instant navigation.** Opening an uncached chat now changes the URL, highlights the item and shows the empty chat in the click itself. The empty chat is the existing `html.chat-url` skeleton that a chat URL already shows while loading. The transcript fills in when the snapshot arrives.

- A later click wins; a stale response is dropped.
- A failed load returns to a new chat with the usual notice, so no skeleton is left behind.
- Typing while a chat opens warms that chat instead of reserving a new draft.
- Sending stays blocked while a chat opens, as before.

**Preview in parallel.** History summaries carry the chat's latest design revision when it is above 0. It is read in the same `HMGET` as the rest of the summary (no extra Redis request), and the transcript summary carries it too. While an uncached chat opens, the preview starts loading that revision. The snapshot then names the same source, so the frame keeps loading instead of starting over. If the chat published a newer design since the list loaded, the preview moves to it when the snapshot arrives.

**Recent chats in the background.** Once per page, when the app is idle after the history arrives, the three most recent other chats load through the same path as hovering one. Opening them then shows their content at once. They stay within the client cache of five chats. Selection already fires on pointer-down (`fastClick`) and focus already prefetches, so neither needed an earlier trigger.

Access is unchanged: the preview route keeps its auth and ownership checks, and the summary only adds a number for chats the user already owns.

## Evidence

Measured on Vercel previews with a headless script. It loads the app fresh, hovers a history item for 300 ms (the app prefetches on hover), clicks it with real input events, and records numbers only. Test chats with a minimal design, 12 samples per side, interleaved in two rounds:

| From the click | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| URL changes (median) | 95 ms | **0.4 ms** |
| Chat shown (median) | 138 ms | **13 ms** |
| Chat content (median) | 138 ms | 156 ms (unchanged within noise) |
| Preview (median) | 618 ms | **558 ms** |
| Preview (worst) | 1501 ms | **690 ms** |

The preview no longer waits for `/api/session`. In one sample `/api/session` took 723 ms (cold) and the preview showed at 453 ms, before the transcript. Whenever the "before" side's `/api/session` was slow, its preview took 1.5 s.

**Realistic chats without hover.** Two test chats with four design turns each, no hover before the click (as on touch or a quick click), and a 3 s pause after load. 8 samples per case:

| Median from the click | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Recent chat: content | 475 ms | **30 ms** (27–31 ms in every sample) |
| Recent chat: preview | 956 ms | **715 ms** |
| Older chat: content | 370 ms | 392 ms (unchanged within noise) |
| Older chat: preview | 901 ms | **602 ms** |

A four-turn chat's `/api/session` response is only 6.5–7 KB (designs are not in the transcript), and the browser takes about 30 ms to process and render it. Chat size is not the bottleneck; the wait for `/api/session` is.

Tried and dropped:

- Moving `/api/session` into the prompt's function made it colder in this setting.
- The 30 s group is unsafe: the route's `DELETE` renews a cleanup lease every 30 s and deletes design assets, so it is built to run longer.
- Moving the fast-snap capture runtime (~95 KB raw per frame) out of each preview needs its own security design, because it would widen the design document's CSP.

## Verification

- `npm run test:core`: 172 passed. It includes a new summary test that fails on the old code.
- `npm run test:auth`: 267 passed. Two UI tests cover choosing New design, or pressing Back to the new-chat page, while a chat opens: the late snapshot no longer replaces the new chat. The New design case also failed on `main`, where that race already existed. A second UI test covers the idle background load (only the three most recent other chats, once per page, then opening from the cache) and fails when the background load is removed. The new UI test covers the URL changing in the click, the empty chat, the later click winning, the failed load, typing while loading and the early preview source. It fails on the old code, and fails when the typing guard or the early preview is removed (checked by mutation).
- `npm run typecheck` and `npm run build`: pass.





Deletion race coverage: deleting a chat while its transcript is still loading now navigates away and discards the late snapshot, including from the client cache. Two regression cases cover another chat remaining and deletion of the last chat, plus Back/Forward to the deleted chat. Both failed before the fix and pass after it. Core (172), auth (267), typecheck, build and diff checks pass locally.

title: Commit the first text without the batch wait and load Blob on first use
body:
## Summary

Two small server changes that make responses start sooner.

- **First text commits without the batch wait.** The projector waited `BATCH_MS` (40 ms) after the first pending line before every commit, even when the previous commit was long ago. It now starts commits at most once per `BATCH_MS` measured from the previous commit, so a line after a quiet spell, such as a turn's first text, commits on the next tick. Lines that follow inside the window still batch together. This applies to every message.
- **`@vercel/blob` loads on first use.** `lib/design-assets.ts` imported `@vercel/blob` at module load. It carries its own undici, jose and the Vercel OIDC client (about 0.6 MB), so every route that imports `lib/agent` or `lib/design-assets` compiled it on a new instance, even for prompts without images. It now loads on the first Blob call. `DesignAssetLimitError` and the image caps are unchanged.

## Measurements

Vercel previews, `main` on both sides with the change only on the candidate.

| Metric | Before | After | Median paired delta | Candidate faster |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| First model chunk to SSE delivery (warm, server clock) | 87 ms | 60 ms | -21 ms | 7/11 |
| First model chunk to projector commit (warm) | 82 ms | 49 ms | -24 ms | 8/11 |
| Projector commits per turn (warm) | 3 | 3 | 0 | |
| `/api/prompt` route module load on a new instance | 165 ms | 103 ms | -63 ms | 10/10 |
| Process uptime when the handler starts (cold, 7 pairs not pre-warmed) | 704 ms | 599 ms | about -110 ms | 7/7 |

Warm rows come from 12 pairs of new chats (11 valid; one baseline capture lost its trace while its prompt completed). Cold rows come from 10 pairs with both sides deployed again before each pair. Browser time to first text is dominated by model and network variance at this sample size, so no browser claim is made for the projector change.

## Tradeoff

The first Blob call on each new instance now pays the load instead: the first image prompt (its uploads already run while libfx admits the prompt), the first image read, and deleting a chat. Warm instances behave as before.

## Validation

- `npm run typecheck`, `npm run test:core` (175), `npm run test:auth` (270), `npm run build`.
- New test: the projector commits a line after a quiet spell at once and batches the lines right behind it; every item lands once and in order. It fails without the change.
- New test: importing `lib/design-assets` does not load `@vercel/blob`, a cleanup with nothing pending does not either, and the first `put` loads it with the same path and options. It fails without the change.

title: Add isolated Ampersand multiplayer design demo
body:
## Summary

Adds **fx0 together**, a self-contained multiplayer design demo at `/ampersand`, built on the Ampersand Agents API. Several people share a room through an invite link, chat together, and an agent edits one shared, versioned HTML page. The agent can stay silent when people are talking to each other, and asks before acting when they disagree.

- Rooms, members, hashed credentials and invites, pending messages, agent sessions, revisions and quotas are stored in Postgres (`ampersand_*` tables).
- One runner per room is coordinated through a database lease, and every agent write is fenced by ownership and the room's input watermark, so the demo works across serverless invocations.
- Quotas, deduplication and member/running-room caps are admitted atomically.
- Generated HTML runs in a network-blocked, opaque-origin sandbox. Links inside a design require confirmation.

## Normal fx0 is unchanged

Existing pages, API routes, auth, journal and migrations `001`–`005` are untouched. Normal fx0 doesn't import the demo runtime or need any of its configuration.

Two existing components gain optional props whose defaults keep current behavior, so the demo can reuse them instead of copying them:

- `components/brand.tsx`: optional `href` (default `/`).
- `components/sidebar.tsx`: optional `homeHref`, `help` and delete callback.

Regression tests cover the defaults, and a production-build smoke test serves normal `/` and its APIs with all demo, auth, Redis and database configuration empty.

## Setup

The demo needs migration `006`, which only creates `ampersand_*` tables:

```sh
psql "$DATABASE_URL" -X -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 --single-transaction -f migrations/006_ampersand_rooms.sql
```

Server environment:

| Variable | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `DATABASE_URL` | Postgres database with migration `006` applied |
| `AMPERSAND_API_KEY` | Key for the Agents API endpoint |
| `AMPERSAND_BASE_URL` | Optional, any HTTPS Agents API-compatible endpoint (default `https://ampersand.humansand.ai/v1`) |
| `AMPERSAND_MODEL` | Optional model id (default `ampersand-v0.1`) |

Public hosting should also set the quota, concurrency and room TTL limits described in `docs/ampersand-collab.md`; they are off by default.

## Verification

- `npm run test:collab` (112), `npm run test:core` (172), `npm run test:auth` (272), `npm run typecheck`, `npm run build`, `npm run test:normal:isolation`, `npm run test:smoke`: all pass.
- `npm run test:collab:postgres` against a disposable local PostgreSQL 18 cluster: 6 concurrency cases with independent connections pass (deduplication, hourly quota, member and run caps, stale-owner and input-watermark fences).

## Not yet verified

- A live session against a real Agents API endpoint with two people in the same room.
- A deployed preview with a real Neon database.

title: Have the agent screenshot its design before claiming it matches a reference
body:
## Summary

The agent rarely called `screenshot_design` on its own, even for "reimplement this exactly" with a reference attached: it published and reported without looking, and said so ("I haven't taken a screenshot to compare it with yours").

The cause was the instructions, not the tool. The system prompt never named `screenshot_design`, its flow ended at "publish, then respond briefly", and the Speed section asks for as few steps as possible. The only nudge was inside the tool description, hedged with "not after every edit" and "on failure, continue without it".

- **Prompt (`lib/agent.ts`).** A new design-mode rule: when the user attaches a reference to match or asks for an exact copy, publish, call `screenshot_design` (with `full_page` when the reference shows more than one screen), compare layout, sizes, spacing and color, fix the differences in one `edit_design`, and only then report. Never claim a match without having looked; say so when the screenshot is unavailable.
- **Tool description (`lib/tools.ts`).** "not after every edit" becomes a concrete rule: use it after publishing when there is a reference or a layout the markup cannot verify; skip it for copy, color or other small edits.

## Tradeoff

Reference and exact-copy turns now pay one capture (about 2 s) and one more model step. Other turns are unchanged. The capture still needs a visible fx0 tab.

## Validation

- `node --experimental-strip-types --test tests/runtime.test.mjs tests/core.test.mjs` (110 pass), including a new test that the rule reaches the prompt's instructions; it fails with the `lib/agent.ts` change reverted.
- `npm run test:core` (177 pass).

title: Let screenshot_design capture at a reference's width
body:
## Summary

`screenshot_design` photographs the preview on screen at the preview's own width. In the split view that is the panel next to the chat, often well under the width a reference was made at (a desktop screenshot is usually 1440 CSS px). The agent then compares two different breakpoints: it "fixes" differences that are only responsive layout, and misses real ones that the narrow layout hides. #42 made the agent compare against references, so this now matters on every reference turn.

- **Tool (`lib/tools.ts`).** An optional `width` (320-1920 CSS px, rounded and clamped by `captureWidth` in `lib/capture-protocol.ts`). The description tells the model to use the reference's width: a 2880-pixel-wide 2x screenshot is 1440.
- **Server and event (`lib/agent.ts`, `lib/events.ts`).** The width travels on the `capture` event as `captureWidth`.
- **Tab (`components/chat-app.tsx`, `components/design-capture.tsx`).** A capture with a width skips the preview and goes straight to the existing hidden copy, at that width instead of 1280. Height stays 800, so `full_page` tiles are unchanged. Without a width nothing changes.
- **Prompt (`lib/agent.ts`).** The reference rule from #42 now says to screenshot "at the width the reference was made at".

## Tradeoff

A width capture always loads the hidden copy, even when the preview already shows the revision. That copy comes from the browser cache for a revision the tab already loaded, so the cost is a paint, not a download.

## Validation

- `npm run test:core` (178 pass), with new tests for `captureWidth` and for the tool passing a rounded, clamped width.
- `npm run typecheck` (exit 0).
- `npm run test:artifact:browser` (42 pass). Its hidden-preview test already captures a 1280 px frame inside a 390 px window, the same path a wider frame takes.
- Not yet checked live: a reference turn should call `screenshot_design` with `width` near the reference's CSS width.

title: Log the sign-in, renewal and sign-out trail with hashed tags
body:
## Summary

Production logged `{"event":"auth:refresh:rejected","status":400,"error":"invalid_grant"}` with nothing to tie it to a user, a login or an earlier exchange. That line can mean a token that outlived its grant (expected) or a rotated token that never reached the browser or Redis (a bug), and the log could not tell them apart.

Every auth line now carries short one-way tags: the first 10 hex characters of SHA-256 (`logTag` in `lib/auth-crypto.ts`) of the user, the login and the refresh token. No token, email or `sub` is logged.

- **Login and sign-out (`app/api/auth/callback`, `app/api/auth/signout`).** `auth:login` (user, login, rt, replaced login) and `auth:signout` (user, login).
- **Exchange (`lib/auth.ts`).** `auth:refresh:exchanged` logs `rt -> next`. The existing `rejected`, `malformed`, `error` and `unavailable` lines now include `rt`.
- **Coordination (`lib/auth.ts`).** `auth:refresh:reused` when a Redis result is replayed, and `auth:refresh:wait_timeout`. `auth:refresh:unpublished` logs a publish that threw or lost its lease. That case was silent before, and it is one way to get `invalid_grant` on another instance.
- **Outcome (`lib/request-session.ts`).** `auth:session:renewed` / `auth:session:ended` with user, login, rt, `sessionAgeS` and `accessExpiresInS`.
- `logRefresh` is replaced by a shared `logAuth` in `lib/auth-protocol.ts`. Successes log at info, failures at error.

## Reading a rejection

Take the `rt` from `auth:session:ended`:

- It appears earlier as the `rt` of an `exchanged` line, or there is an `unpublished` line for it: the token had already been used. Either a stale cookie came back or Redis did not keep the result.
- It appears only as a `next` or in `auth:login`, and `sessionAgeS` is large: the grant expired or was revoked at Vercel.

## Verification

All exited 0:

- `npm run test:auth`: 271/271 passed. A new test runs a renewal followed by a rejection of the rotated token. It asserts the `exchanged -> renewed -> rejected -> ended` chain is linked by tags and that no token, `sub` or email appears in the output.
- `npm run test:core`: 178/178 passed.
- `npm run typecheck`
- `npm run build`
- `git diff --check`

Not yet checked on a deployment: the lines should appear in Vercel runtime logs on a real sign-in and renewal.
