title: Embed Google Fonts in designs before they run
body:
## Goal

Let designs use Google Fonts for English and Spanish without giving generated code network access. The agent writes ordinary Google Fonts stylesheet links or imports; fx0 downloads the Latin WOFF2 faces on the server and embeds them as data URLs.

## Implementation

- Allow Google Fonts stylesheet links and preconnect hints in authored HTML. Separate those stylesheet references from image URL handling.
- Rebuild bounded `@font-face` rules from allowlisted descriptors; do not forward Google's raw CSS into the document. Deduplicate files and merge repeated variable weights.
- Prepare fonts for both the preview and copied/downloaded HTML, including historical revisions. Remove recognized external font references when loading fails or downloads are disabled, leaving the CSS fallback stack rather than an external dependency.
- Preserve source HTML for exact edits and prepare a separate render copy. Keep the existing sandbox and `font-src data:` / `connect-src 'none'` policies.
- Reuse the shared Runtime Cache and warm it during generation. Failed or incomplete downloads throw instead of being cached as missing font styles for a day.
- Bound each stylesheet to 16 files, four font downloads in flight, 256 KiB per file, 512 KiB embedded font bytes, and one five-second deadline covering CSS and files. The final rendered design has a 768 KiB font-CSS budget.
- Keep the existing `FX0_REMOTE_IMAGES=0` control. No new DB schema, asset store, font catalog, or runtime font connections.
- Merge current main, preserving #49/#50 and #51's screenshot scale corrections. Update the agent instructions and publish tool description consistently.

## Security review

Reviewed the current implementation statically, with an independent read-only review, and exercised the relevant negative tests. No material security blockers were found within this scope.

- **Outbound requests:** enforce the exact expected HTTPS origin before every hop's DNS lookup and connection, including redirects and alternate ports. Retain public-address validation, pinned DNS, credential rejection and TLS hostname verification.
- **CSS/HTML injection:** rebuild only supported font descriptors with constrained values and base64 bytes; raw upstream CSS is not injected. Embedded font CSS cannot close a style element.
- **Resource limits:** bound response bytes, file count, concurrency, total download time and serialized output. Do not cache transient total or partial download failures.
- **Browser isolation:** generated scripts get no new network capability, app-origin access or cookies. Real Chrome tests verify fonts and captures under the unchanged CSP.
- **Export authorization:** reuse the ownership-protected artifact route, keeping plain-text attachment, private-cache, sandbox and nosniff response headers.

Residual risks: font files still rely on Google's provenance and the browser's font decoder; the WOFF2 signature check is not a structural font audit. Downloaded model-generated HTML remains untrusted active content when opened independently. The parser intentionally handles the supported font-link/import syntax rather than being a general HTML/CSS sanitizer.

## Scope and limitations

Latin fonts for English and Spanish are intentional; this PR does not promise other writing systems. History preserves HTML, not immutable snapshots of external resources. The Google CSS query can resolve to different font files after cache revalidation, just as existing remote images can change. A successfully exported font is embedded in that downloaded file. Unavailable or over-budget styles fall back to the authored CSS font stack.

## Review follow-up (91460bc)

Both review comments were reproduced with failing regression tests before the fixes:

- Font-bearing previews no longer use revision-only ETags. They return `private, no-store` and ignore stale revision validators, so reloading after a transient failure retries font preparation without editing the source. Designs without font dependencies retain their fast 304 path. The server-side font cache is unchanged.
- Embedded faces only reuse an unconditional CSS style, skipping restricted media, non-CSS type, disabled and titled styles. When none is eligible, a new unconditional style is inserted rather than changing the authored restrictions. That DOM-shape change safely uses full preview reloads instead of hot updates.

The Chrome test exercises restricted first styles, the no-eligible-style case, screenshots and offline export with a real WOFF2 fixture. Current verification counts are listed below.

## Verification

| Command / check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `npm run -s test:core` | 199/199 pass, exit 0 |
| `npm run -s test:auth` | 276/276 pass, exit 0 |
| `npm run -s test:artifact:browser` | 43/43 pass, exit 0 |
| `npm run -s typecheck` | exit 0 |
| `git diff --check` | exit 0 |

The browser suite now contains a deterministic real WOFF2 fixture with its OFL license. It verifies that the custom font actually loads and differs from a monospace fallback, appears in screenshot glyph widths, survives a hot style edit and historical reload, and matches the offline export at the same 800 CSS px viewport, without CSP violations.

Live Google check: Inter 400/700 + Playfair Display 700 produced two embedded faces and 96,313 bytes of CSS in about 1.5 s on the instrumented run, without external font URLs. A preceding attempt hit the five-second deadline; this is a bounded fallback/retry condition, not a latency guarantee. No live-model or production-database integration test was run.

title: Return SVG, XML, JSON and CSS from web_fetch as is
body:
## Problem

`web_fetch` stripped every tag from every response, so an SVG came back empty. In a real session ("use the real svg" for the Name.com logo), `https://www.name.com/_nuxt/name_logo.4-FjecQ7.svg` returned `status 200` with `content: ""`. The agent then tried third-party proxies (codetabs, allorigins), three of which hit the 20 s budget or returned 522, and gave up until the user pasted the SVG by hand.

## Change

- `fetchPublic` returns the response's `content-type`.
- `web_fetch` reduces a response to text only when it is HTML (`text/html`, `application/xhtml+xml`). SVG, XML, JSON, CSS and other text come back as is, under the same size cap. With no content type, a body starting with `<svg` or `<?xml` is kept; anything else is treated as a page, as before.
- Binary responses (images, PDFs, fonts, `application/octet-stream`) return an error naming the type instead of their bytes decoded as text, which only filled the context.
- The tool description says so, so the agent knows it can place a fetched SVG inline.

## Security

SSRF checks are unchanged (public addresses only, DNS pinned, every redirect revalidated, size and time limits). Raw markup reaches the tool widget as React text in a `<pre>`, so it is escaped. An SVG placed in a design goes through the same artifact validator and sandboxed, no-connection CSP as any other design markup.

## Verification

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `npm run test:core` | 181 of 181 pass, including new cases for SVG with and without a content type, XML, JSON, JSON-LD, CSS, HTML with a content type, and binary types |
| `npm run typecheck` | exit 0 |
| Merged together with #50 locally | no conflicts; `test:core` 182 of 182, typecheck exit 0 |

title: Preserve screenshot dimensions and avoid rebuilding references as miniatures
body:
## Goal

A user captures a UI, attaches or pastes it, and asks fx0 to recreate it at the same visual scale: text, controls, spacing and columns, not a miniature with similar proportions.

## Diagnosis and limits

The composer resizes attachments to at most 2048 px (sometimes smaller). Previously the agent was not told the original dimensions, while its instructions encouraged inferring 2x/3x from text in the image. That loses useful information and can produce a wrong scale. This is a plausible explanation of the reported small designs, not a confirmed diagnosis of the exact reference: we have not compared the user's original file and generated HTML in a controlled real-model run.

Pixels alone do not tell us a screenshot's CSS viewport. A filename's @1x/@2x/@3x is a hint, and a crop may show only part of a viewport. Pasted images can have no density information at all.

## Changes

- Keep each original file's dimensions through normalization, including pasted images. Only infer a density hint when the filename explicitly says @1x, @2x or @3x. Do not retain or send the filename.
- Share bounded numeric source validation between prompt admission and the sign-in draft. Compare source dimensions with the transmitted image's actual headers; discard implausible metadata without rejecting the image. Keep old drafts readable and preserve source metadata through sign-in.
- Tell the model the original and transmitted dimensions separately. Label filename-derived density as a hint and missing density as unknown. Do not equate a captured region with a full CSS viewport, or claim transmitted dimensions are necessarily what the model sees after provider resizing.
- Replace the blanket Retina heuristic: do not assume 2x/3x because an image is large, a screenshot, or from CleanShot. Preserve on-screen scale as well as proportions, use explicit user sizes first, and avoid shrinking the whole design to fit the preview.
- Clarify screenshot verification: use the reference's CSS viewport when known, otherwise the visible preview width. Compare text/control sizes and spacing at a common CSS scale, not by independently fitting both images to thumbnails. Capture again after correcting the result.

The image parts sent to libfx, network access controls and capture implementation are unchanged.

## Verification

| Command | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `npm run -s test:core` | 186/186 pass, exit 0 |
| `npm run -s test:auth` | 273/273 pass, exit 0 |
| `npm run -s typecheck` | exit 0 |
| `node --experimental-strip-types --test tests/attach-image.browser.mjs` | 1/1 pass in real headless Chrome, exit 0; resized files preserve original size, @1x/@2x/@3x names keep hints, and a nameless pasted file gets no invented density |
| `git diff --check` | exit 0 |

Tests also cover source metadata surviving sign-in, old drafts, invalid metadata, tall captures with rounding, unknown density, and the message actually delivered through submitPrompt.

## Still required: real-model visual check

On the preview, recreate the same reference by dragging the CleanShot file and by pasting it. Repeat with sign-in between attachment and send. Check generated text/control sizes and spacing against the reference at a common CSS scale, not only an announced pixel width. This visual behavior has not yet been verified with a real model; passing transport/prompt tests is not proof of visual fidelity.

title: Recover rotated auth sessions and add redacted diagnostics
body:
## Summary

- Recover a valid login when its browser sends an older, already-rotated credential. Keep the latest token state encrypted per login in the existing Redis instance instead of relying only on the short-lived refresh-result cache.
- Use exact-state compare-and-set publication, adopt the winning generation after concurrent refreshes, and fence reads and writes with the existing permanent logout marker.
- If publication fails after a successful provider exchange, preserve the encrypted successor credential for retry and return a retryable response without dispatching the protected handler.
- Add session diagnostics covering incoming credentials, durable-state selection, publication outcomes and final prepared cookie headers. Document-local page context distinguishes visibility and prerender hints without becoming an authentication signal.
- Use 96-bit, purpose- and kind-separated HMAC fingerprints derived from `SESSION_SECRET`. Do not log raw credentials, cookies, authorization headers, query strings or exception details. No additional environment variable is required.

- Bind pending publication to the consumed token as well as the prior raw seal. Repair a resealed predecessor with bounded CAS retries, preserving the live pending successor on contention. Cover the delayed-bootstrap race with one-hour tokens.

- Delete the login-wide encrypted credential during existing sign-out cleanup, including logins with no chats. Keep the permanent revocation marker and other logins' credentials intact; late refresh publication remains fenced.

- Keep renewal decisions explicit rather than inferring them from serialized cookies, share the credential key definition between publication and cleanup, and isolate diagnostic details in local helpers. Existing regression tests and recovery semantics remain unchanged.

## Verification

Node 24.22.1 and Next.js 16.4.2. All final checks exited 0:

- `npm run test:auth`: 325 passed.
- `npm run test:core`: 199 passed.
- `npm run typecheck`.
- `npm run build`.
- `git diff --check`.

The stale-cookie regression fails with the previous request wrapper and passes with this change. Tests cover multiple generations after cache expiry, late publication, terminal-result races, persistence outages, pending-publication recovery, logout fencing, sealed-record binding, fixed retention, HMAC separation and diagnostic redaction. Provider and Redis REST responses are synthetic; no live credentials or production logs are included.

## Operational notes

- Uses existing Redis and session-secret configuration; no database migration.
- Durable token retention is renewed only by successful provider exchanges, not reads. Successful sign-out cleanup deletes that login's encrypted credential; the permanent revocation marker remains effective while background cleanup is pending or unavailable. Cookie identity and team selection retain their existing owners.
- This prevents an older credential from causing the observed refresh failure; it does not establish why a browser originally retained or restored that credential. Prepared cookie headers are not proof of browser acceptance.
- A successor credential lost before this change cannot be reconstructed; affected existing logins may need to sign in again.
- Pending cookies issued before consumed-token binding still repair exact predecessors and recognize an already-stored successor. Other ambiguous state changes retain the pending credential and return 503; those old ambiguous grants may require signing in again.
- Real-provider sign-in/renewal and the Redis Lua scripts still need deployment verification. Do not roll back to a serving version that ignores the durable credential record after adoption.
- Runtime logs remain pseudonymous operational data. Review access and retention in the hosting provider; do not post production logs in public issues or PRs.

title: Reduce screenshot startup and delivery latency
body:
## Summary

- Match `/api/capture`'s `maxDuration = 800` to prompt/warm so uploads can reuse their function pool. This permits reuse; it does not guarantee instance affinity.
- Start journal and draft reads together, but deliver ready journal events before awaiting the draft. A pending draft read no longer holds an already-available capture request.
- Poll active turns at 50–75 ms instead of 100–150 ms. Preserve the existing idle reset/backoff.
- Add numeric capture `Server-Timing`, an application instance marker, capture-only delivery diagnostics, and regression coverage. Clarify that cross-machine timing estimates are not pure network latency.

No new endpoints, dependencies, Redis blocking readers, ACK changes, image-quality changes, or auth/ownership changes. The experimental Redis wake channel and encoder changes are excluded.

## Measurements

Manual investigation on November 6, 2026; these are scoped experiments, not universal latency guarantees.

### Real capture pipeline

24 balanced randomized A/B pairs (48 measured captures after four warmups), using the real PreviewPane, renderer, upload/auth route, and Redis reply path. Same design/revision, 1000×720 viewport and 16,518-byte image throughout.

| Metric | Previous delivery | Journal-first / faster active polling |
|---|---:|---:|
| Capture median | 424.63 ms | 363.79 ms |
| Capture p90 | 489.94 ms | 420.81 ms |
| Upload HTTP median | 293.65 ms | 296.65 ms |

The capture median decreased by about 61 ms (14%) on this fixture/network path. The paired capture difference had a median of −64.13 ms, with an exploratory bootstrap interval of [−112.44, −31.78] ms. This measures the core capture pipeline, not complete LLM-turn latency.

### Function-pool startup

Fresh preview deployments, prime prompt, then issue two concurrent capture requests. Repeated with variant order reversed. These deliberately return 401 to isolate bootstrap: they are **not full screenshot measurements**. All eight requests used the same `gru1` edge / `iad1` function regions.

| Trial | Separate capture config | Matching prompt config |
|---|---|---|
| Control then candidate | 1 prewarmed + 1 cold; cold TTFB 1204 ms | 2 hot; max TTFB 77 ms |
| Candidate then control | 1 prewarmed + 1 cold; cold TTFB 1131 ms | 2 hot; max TTFB 43 ms |

These provider start classifications support warm-pool reuse under the tested condition, not a production p95 claim. Matching config alone does not keep instances hot. Client timing trials with anomalous parallel response completion were excluded from latency claims.

## Tradeoffs and limits

Active polling frequency roughly doubles; idle polling is unchanged. No additional persistent Redis connection is introduced.

This does not fix every slow capture. The investigated production deployment had 5 cold invocations among 185 ack/photo requests, while 22 of 92 successful capture traces still exceeded one second after subtracting preview wait. Some slow cases occurred with hot functions and remain outside this change's claim.

## Verification

On Node 24:
- Focused stream/capture/security/runtime/transcript suite: **123 passed**.
- `npm run test:core`: **212 passed**.
- `npm run test:auth`: **325 passed**.
- `next typegen` and `tsc --noEmit --incremental false`: **passed**.
- `next build`: **passed**.
- `git diff --check`: **passed**.

Regression coverage includes journal/draft completion order, ready capture delivery with a pending draft, cancellation/terminal closure with late draft resolution or rejection, active/idle polling cadence, delivery deduplication, function configuration, and diagnostic headers. No production deployment is included.

title: Offer free prompts only to visitors, once per network
body:
## Summary

- Sponsor only visitors without an account. A signed-in user always bills their own team on every model, in a new, reserved or existing chat, including chats that began as a trial. Before this, a signed-in user who picked Opus 5.5 Fast in a new design spent the visitor allowance and saw "N free prompts left".

A connection can send from any address in its /64, so per-address counting gave the same person a fresh allowance whenever their address changed. An IPv4-mapped IPv6 address counts as its IPv4 address. Fixes #22.

title: Retry a refused sign-in once through Vercel's consent page
body:
## Summary

- When a user has already authorized fx0, Vercel's authorize endpoint skips the consent page. If the token it returns has no team that AI Gateway accepts, the callback showed "Choose a Vercel team with AI Gateway access to continue." The user then had to press Continue with Vercel, which adds `prompt=consent`, to reach the team picker and sign in.
- The OAuth flow cookie now records whether the sign-in forced consent. A callback that finds no Gateway team redirects once to `/api/auth/signin?reauth=true`. A sign-in that already forced consent still shows the error, so the retry cannot loop.
- The refusal is logged as `auth:callback:no-gateway-team`. The event records the keyed user, whether consent was forced, whether it retried, the count of teams per probe status, and up to 20 probes with the keyed team and Gateway's scrubbed error `type`, `code` and `message`. Tokens, raw team IDs, raw user IDs and raw response bodies are never logged. The event appears only in the project's runtime logs.
- `logTag` gains a `team` domain, and the README's sign-out diagnostics section documents the new event.

## Evidence from production logs

Between Nov 10 and Nov 18 there were two `team_access` failures. Both came from sign-ins without `reauth`, and both users signed in on their next attempt with `reauth=true`. No sign-in with `reauth=true` ended in `team_access`. On Nov 18 the sequence was:

| UTC | Event |
| --- | --- |
| 01:55:15 | `/api/auth/signin`, no `reauth` |
| 01:55:43 | `auth:callback:failed`: "Grant a Vercel team with AI Gateway access" |
| 02:01:13 | `/api/auth/signin?reauth=true` from the same browser |
| 02:09:50 | `auth:login` succeeds |

The user's screen recording shows Vercel asking only for passkey identity confirmation before redirecting, with no team picker. The logs cannot show why no team was accepted. A team that requires a fresh SAML SSO grant is the leading explanation, and the new log event will confirm or rule it out on the next failure.

## Verification

All checks exited 0:

- `npm run typecheck`
- `npm run test:auth`: 326 passed.
- `npm run test:core`: 199 passed.
- `npm run build`
- `git diff --check`

New and updated tests cover the retry without prior consent, the error after forced consent, a malformed `consent` value in the flow cookie, the `consent` value that `/api/auth/signin` seals with and without `reauth`, the logged probe details, and the absence of the token, raw team IDs and the raw user ID from the log. The callback test mock now answers the JWKS request itself instead of relying on an earlier test's cache.

I ran the production build locally with `next start` and checked `/api/auth/signin` over HTTP. Without `reauth` it redirects to Vercel without `prompt` and seals `consent: false`. With `reauth=true` it sends `prompt=consent` and seals `consent: true`. Both include `teamSelection=single-team`. The full callback against Vercel OAuth was not exercised locally; on the preview, sign in with an account whose team requires SSO and confirm that a refused first attempt continues to the consent page.
